name: Stonefield Castle

tagline: William Playfair's 1837 Baronial mansion above Loch Fyne, where the Barmore Bistro has explicitly welcomed non-residents and hotel guests alike since 1950
highlights: Built in 1837 to a design by the noted architect William Playfair, on the site of the earlier Barmore House
The original Barmore House was built by the Clan MacAlister, tenants of Tarbert Castle under the Duke of Argyll
The Barmore estate was bought in 1746 by Archibald Campbell, Sheriff of Argyll — it was his great-great-grandson who developed the derelict early-19th-century house into the current castle
Set in 60 acres of woodland with panoramic views over Loch Fyne
A hotel since 1950, retaining original furnishings, wood panelling, ornate ceilings and marble fireplaces — with the Barmore Bistro explicitly open to residents and non-residents year-round
description:
Stonefield Castle stands above Loch Fyne on Argyll's Kintyre peninsula, near the small town of Tarbert, and its site carries a longer history than the current building itself, which dates to 1837. Before Stonefield, the site was occupied by an earlier house known as Barmore House, built by the Clan MacAlister, who held the land as tenants of Tarbert Castle under the Duke of Argyll — a tenancy arrangement typical of the layered landholding structures that shaped so much of Highland and Argyll estate history. In 1746, Archibald Campbell, Sheriff of Argyll, purchased the Barmore estate, but it was not Archibald himself who transformed the property into the castle visitors see today; that development fell to his great-great-grandson, who took the deteriorated early-19th-century house in hand and commissioned its rebuilding.

The result was designed by William Playfair, one of the most significant Scottish architects of the 19th century, working in the Scottish Baronial style that would come to define so much of the country's grand domestic architecture in this period. Playfair's Stonefield, completed in 1837, replaced the earlier deteriorated house with a substantial Baronial mansion set within 60 acres of surrounding woodland, positioned to take full advantage of its panoramic views over Loch Fyne — one of Scotland's longest sea lochs, and a defining feature of this stretch of the Argyll coastline.

Stonefield has operated as a hotel since 1950, and unusually for a conversion of this vintage, it has retained a striking amount of its original 19th-century character: original furnishings, wood panelling, ornately decorated ceilings and marble fireplaces remain throughout the public rooms, giving the interior a genuine sense of continuity with Playfair's original design rather than a wholesale modern reinvention.

The grounds surrounding the castle are as notable as the building itself. Loch Fyne's position on Argyll's west coast puts Stonefield's 60 acres within reach of the mild, moisture-laden microclimate carried inland by the Gulf Stream, and the estate's gardens have made use of this over the decades to grow rhododendrons and other plant species that would struggle considerably further inland or further north — a horticultural tradition shared with several other west-coast Argyll estates, where sheltered sea-loch settings allow genuinely unusual planting for this latitude. Woodland paths through the estate lead down toward the loch shore, giving guests and visitors a reason to explore well beyond the castle's public rooms.

What sets Stonefield apart most clearly among Scotland's castle-hotels, however, is the explicitness of its public access. The Barmore Bistro is described in the hotel's own materials as open to residents and non-residents alike, year-round — language considerably more direct than the more cautious or partial access found at some comparable properties. The bar follows the same policy, open to both residents and non-residents until 11pm. The hotel's own breakfast menu goes a step further still, carrying a dedicated section for 'Non-Residents & Room Only Package bookings,' priced at £17.95 per person — a level of structured, deliberate non-resident access that few Scottish castle-hotels state so plainly. Afternoon Tea is served Monday to Saturday, from 12:30pm to 4pm, in the castle's drawing room, rounding out a genuinely comprehensive day-visitor offer built around dining rather than any single showcase event.

For travellers exploring the Kintyre peninsula, or breaking a journey between Argyll's mainland and the ferries serving Islay and the wider Hebrides, Stonefield's position above Loch Fyne — combined with its unusually open approach to non-resident dining — makes it one of the most accessible castle-hotel experiences in this part of Scotland, whether or not a room is booked.
history: The site of Stonefield Castle was previously occupied by Barmore House, built by the Clan MacAlister as tenants of Tarbert Castle under the Duke of Argyll. Archibald Campbell, Sheriff of Argyll, purchased the Barmore estate in 1746, and it was his great-great-grandson who developed the deteriorated early-19th-century house into the current castle, commissioning a rebuilding to a design by the architect William Playfair, completed in 1837 in the Scottish Baronial style. The castle has operated as a hotel since 1950, retaining much of its original furnishing, wood panelling, ornamented ceilings and marble fireplaces.

faqs.question: Can I eat at Stonefield Castle without staying overnight?
faqs.answer: Yes, very clearly. The Barmore Bistro is explicitly open to both residents and non-residents year-round, as is the hotel bar, which welcomes non-residents until 11pm. The hotel's own breakfast menu even includes a dedicated 'Non-Residents & Room Only Package bookings' section priced at £17.95 per person, and Afternoon Tea is served in the drawing room Monday to Saturday, 12:30pm to 4pm.

faqs.question: Who designed Stonefield Castle?
faqs.answer: Stonefield Castle was designed by William Playfair, a leading Scottish architect of the 19th century, and completed in 1837 in the Scottish Baronial style. It replaced an earlier, deteriorated house called Barmore House that had stood on the same site.

faqs.question: What is the history of the land Stonefield Castle stands on?
faqs.answer: The site was originally home to Barmore House, built by the Clan MacAlister, who held the land as tenants of Tarbert Castle under the Duke of Argyll. Archibald Campbell, Sheriff of Argyll, bought the Barmore estate in 1746, and it was his great-great-grandson who eventually redeveloped the site into the current Stonefield Castle in the early 19th century.

faqs.question: Why does Stonefield Castle have unusual plants in its gardens?
faqs.answer: Stonefield's 60 acres sit on the shore of Loch Fyne, within reach of the mild, moisture-laden microclimate the Gulf Stream carries along Argyll's west coast. This allows the estate's gardens to grow rhododendrons and other species that would typically struggle at this latitude further inland — a tradition shared with several other sheltered west-coast Argyll estates, and a rewarding detail for guests who explore the woodland paths down toward the loch shore.
